beats.speaker: tilly-space
beats.voiceover: We're over a billion kilometres from home, above Saturn's north pole. No landing, by the way. Saturn has no solid surface to stand on.

shots.place: Saturn's north pole seen from high above: a huge golden hexagon of cloud circling the pole, with exactly six long straight sides and six sharp corners, a deep blue swirling storm at the very centre, the edge of the planet curving away into black space
shots.action: looks out through the round cabin window, slowly drifting closer to the glass
shots.line: We're over a billion kilometres from home, above Saturn's north pole.
shots.sound: the soft hum of cabin fans

shots.place: inside a small, slightly shabby budget tourist spacecraft cabin: padded off-white walls, a big round window, soft cabin light; Saturn's banded golden clouds filling the window behind her
shots.line: No landing, by the way. Saturn has no solid surface to stand on.

beats.speaker: tilly-space
beats.voiceover: First, the shape. A six-sided storm, and each side is wider than Earth. The wind racing along its edge? Over three hundred kilometres an hour. And it's not new. Voyager spotted it in the early eighties. Cassini found it still there, decades later.

shots.place: Saturn's north pole seen from high above: a huge golden hexagon of cloud circling the pole, with exactly six long straight sides and six sharp corners, a deep blue swirling storm at the very centre, the edge of the planet curving away into black space

shots.line: First, the shape. A six-sided storm, and each side is wider than Earth.

shots.place: close view of one straight edge of Saturn's golden six-sided hexagon: long streaks of cloud racing along a straight band, darker and lighter stripes on either side

shots.line: The wind racing along its edge? Over three hundred kilometres an hour.
shots.sound: the soft hum of cabin fans

shots.place: the whole of Saturn's north pole with the golden six-sided hexagon in the middle, the thin bright rings arcing across the bottom of the frame, black space all around

beats.speaker: tilly-space
beats.voiceover: The catch? Nobody's totally sure why it has six sides. Lab tanks of spinning water make shapes like it. And the south pole? No hexagon. Weird.

claims.claim: Saturn has a long-lasting six-sided (hexagonal) cloud pattern around its north pole.
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn%27s_hexagon ; NASA/JPL, 'Saturn's Mysterious Hexagon Emerges From Winter Darkness' (2009), https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/saturns-mysterious-hexagon-emerges-from-winter-darkness/
claims.note: Also the on-screen hook text 'Saturn's hexagon'. The hexagon sits at about 78° N.

claims.claim: Saturn is more than a billion kilometres from Earth.
claims.source: NASA Saturn facts (about 1.4 billion km from the Sun), https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/facts/ ; ESA Facts about Saturn
claims.note: Earth–Saturn distance varies from roughly 1.2 to 1.7 billion km; 'over a billion' is true at all times.

claims.claim: Saturn is a gas giant with no solid surface to stand on.
claims.source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Saturn: 'As a gas giant, Saturn doesn't have a true surface', https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/facts/ ; ESA Facts about Saturn
claims.note: It may have a solid core deep inside, but nothing a visitor could land on.

claims.claim: Each side of the hexagon is longer than Earth's diameter (about 13,800–14,500 km per side vs Earth's 12,742 km).
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn%27s_hexagon (sides about 14,500 km) ; Astronomy magazine, 'Weird object: Hexagon on Saturn' (2015), https://www.astronomy.com/science/weird-object-hexagon-on-saturn/ (13,800 km)
claims.note: Sources give 13,800 or 14,500 km per side; both exceed Earth's diameter, so the line says only 'wider than Earth'.

claims.claim: The jet stream along the hexagon blows at roughly 100 metres per second, over 300 km/h.
claims.source: NASA/JPL (2009) hexagon release: jet stream at about 100 m/s (220 mph), https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/saturns-mysterious-hexagon-emerges-from-winter-darkness/ ; Space.com, https://www.space.com/7651-saturn-weird-hexagon-images.html
claims.note: 100 m/s = 360 km/h, 220 mph = 354 km/h; said conservatively as 'over three hundred kilometres an hour'.

claims.claim: The hexagon was discovered in Voyager images in the early 1980s, and NASA's Cassini spacecraft imaged it again decades later.
claims.source: NASA/JPL (2009): 'originally discovered in images taken by the Voyager spacecraft in the early 1980s' and Cassini's matching images, https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/saturns-mysterious-hexagon-emerges-from-winter-darkness/

claims.claim: Scientists are not fully sure why the hexagon has six sides; spinning-water lab experiments produce similar polygon shapes.
claims.source: Barbosa Aguiar, Read et al., 'A laboratory model of Saturn's North Polar Hexagon', Icarus 206 (2010); Smithsonian Magazine, https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/saturns-polar-hexagon-26686194/ ; Rostami et al., Icarus 297 (2017): 'not enough convincing dynamical explanation', https://web.lmd.jussieu.fr/~aspiga/pub/REF/2017Icar..297...59R.pdf
claims.note: A meandering jet stream is the leading explanation, but it is debated; said as 'nobody's totally sure'.

claims.claim: Saturn's south pole has no matching hexagon.
claims.source: Rostami et al., Icarus 297 (2017) on 'the absence of its counterpart at Saturn's South pole', https://web.lmd.jussieu.fr/~aspiga/pub/REF/2017Icar..297...59R.pdf ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn%27s_hexagon
claims.note: The south pole has a large polar vortex (hurricane-like storm), but no hexagon.

publish.title: I floated over Saturn's hexagon
publish.description: A six-sided storm, each side wider than Earth, winds over 300 km/h, and nobody is totally sure why it's a hexagon. Tilly reviews Saturn's north pole.
